title: Data from Information Repositories: Databases
summary: Databases concentrate the records an organisation depends on, so this sub-technique is the parent behaviour aimed at structured data stores, whether self hosted or delivered as a managed cloud service. Targets range from relational systems to document and analytics platforms, and the data of interest includes usernames, hashed passwords, personal information and financial records. Collection can happen through the normal database protocol with a valid account, through an application that already holds credentials, through an administration console, or through a cloud storage location the database uses for exports. Because legitimate applications generate constant query traffic, defenders rarely spot the read itself and must instead look at volume, shape and origin: queries returning far more rows than usual, exports or copies to an unexpected destination, newly created accounts or keys, access from a host that normally does not talk to the database, and large transfers out of the environment. The strongest signal is a change in the pattern of access rather than any single statement.

beginner.definition: A database is an organised store of information, such as customer records or payment details. This sub-technique means an attacker reads that store in order to steal data. It is the parent idea, aimed at databases rather than documents or chat. The attacker often uses a normal account or a stolen key.
beginner.whyItMatters: Databases usually hold the most valuable and most personal data a company has. Losing it can lead to fraud, fines and lost trust. Applications query databases all day long, so strange reads hide in the noise. Attackers often copy a whole table instead of a few records. This makes it a serious and hard to see form of theft.
howItWorks: The parent technique covers shared repositories in general; this one targets databases.
The attacker finds a valid database account, an application key or an open service.
They connect to it directly, or they abuse an application that already trusts them.
They list the tables and columns to find names, emails and payment fields.
They run a query that returns far more rows than normal use would ever return.
They copy the results to a system outside the company, sometimes in several stages.
beginner.example: Think of a warehouse that keeps every order in labelled crates. Staff collect a few crates all day, so the forklifts are always moving and nobody watches them. A driver with a valid pass quietly loads a whole aisle onto a truck at night. The gate log shows a normal employee and a normal truck, because every check was passed. Only the size of the load was unusual.
takeaways: Databases hold the most sensitive records, so the size of a read matters a lot.
Constant application traffic hides theft, so compare patterns rather than single queries.
Watch for large exports and for hosts that never normally reach the database.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique narrows the parent technique to databases.
List the kinds of data commonly targeted during database collection.
Describe the access paths an adversary may use to reach a database.
Identify volume and origin signals that indicate bulk data collection.
Outline controls that limit unnecessary exposure of database contents.
